about: Sourced life stories for Israel's neighbours: three kings of Syria named Ben-hadad, Hazael, Rezin, Hiram of Tyre, Mesha of Moab, the queen of Sheba and Candace. Written from Scripture and the reviewed dossier Research/People/rulers-neighbours.md.

ben-hadad-1ki-15-18.short: Ben-hadad son of Tabrimon, king of Syria at Damascus, took Asa's silver and gold to break his league with Baasha; Kings also tells of a Ben-hadad who fought Ahab.

paragraphs.text: Kings names him “Ben-hadad, the son of Tabrimon, the son of Hezion, king of Syria, that dwelt at Damascus”. Baasha king of Israel was building Ramah against Asa king of Judah, so Asa took all the silver and gold left in the treasures of the house of the LORD and of the king's house, and sent it to him. Asa's message spoke of a league “between my father and thy father”, and asked Ben-hadad to break his league with Baasha.

Ben-hadad “hearkened unto king Asa”, and his captains struck Ijon, Dan, Abel-beth-maachah, all Cinneroth and all the land of Naphtali. When Baasha heard of it he left off building Ramah, and Asa carried away its stones and timber to build Geba and Mizpah. Chronicles tells the same story, sets it in the thirty-sixth year of Asa's reign, and names Abel-maim and the store cities of Naphtali. It adds that the seer Hanani rebuked Asa for relying on the king of Syria and not on the LORD.

In Ahab's reign “Ben-hadad the king of Syria” gathered all his host, with thirty-two kings, and besieged Samaria. He claimed Ahab's silver and gold, wives and children, and then said his servants would search Ahab's house and the houses of his servants. When Ahab, on the elders' advice, refused the second demand, Ben-hadad swore that the dust of Samaria would not be enough for handfuls for all his people. Kings never names the father of this Ben-hadad, and Scripture does not say whether he is the son of Tabrimon whom Asa paid.

While he was “drinking himself drunk in the pavilions” with the kings, the young men of the princes of the provinces came out of Samaria; the Syrians fled, and he escaped on a horse with the horsemen. His servants told him that Israel's gods were “gods of the hills”, and at the return of the year he went up to Aphek to fight in the plain. There Israel slew a hundred thousand Syrian footmen in one day, a wall fell on twenty-seven thousand more, and Ben-hadad fled into an inner chamber of the city.

His servants went out to Ahab in sackcloth with ropes on their heads: “Thy servant Ben-hadad saith, I pray thee, let me live.” Ahab answered, “he is my brother”, took him up into his chariot, and sent him away with a covenant, after Ben-hadad promised to restore the cities “which my father took from thy father”. A man of the sons of the prophets then told Ahab that the LORD had appointed this man “to utter destruction”, and that Ahab's life would go for his.

Scripture gives this king no length of reign and no account of his death. In 1 Kings 22 the king of Syria whose captains fought Ahab at Ramoth-gilead is not named. Jeremiah, speaking of Damascus, says a fire “shall consume the palaces of Ben-hadad”; the verse names no king of its own day. When he reigned, and whether the Ben-hadads are one man or more, are set out on his page as a ruler.

ben-hadad-2ki-6-24.short: Ben-hadad king of Syria besieged Samaria in Elisha's day, and later, sick in Damascus, sent Hazael to ask Elisha whether he would recover; Hazael reigned after him.

paragraphs.text: Scripture names this Ben-hadad in two passages of 2 Kings, and gives neither his father nor the length of his reign. The chapters just before the first of them speak of “the king of Syria” without naming him: Naaman's master, and the king who warred against Israel and sent a great host to fetch Elisha from Dothan. They do not say whether that king is this Ben-hadad. Nor does Scripture say whether he is the Ben-hadad who fought Ahab in 1 Kings 20.

After this “Ben-hadad king of Syria gathered all his host, and went up, and besieged Samaria.” There was a great famine in the city, until an ass's head was sold for eighty pieces of silver, and a woman cried to the king on the wall that she and her neighbour had agreed to eat their sons. The king rent his clothes, the people saw that he had sackcloth on his flesh beneath, and he swore that Elisha's head would not stay on him that day. The story calls him only “the king of Israel”.

Elisha said that by the next day a measure of fine flour would be sold for a shekel in the gate of Samaria. In the twilight four lepers went out to the Syrian camp and found it empty: the Lord had made the Syrians hear “a noise of chariots, and a noise of horses”, and they had fled for their lives, saying the king of Israel had hired the kings of the Hittites and of the Egyptians against them. The way to the Jordan was full of the garments and vessels they had cast away, and flour was sold for a shekel, “according to the word of the LORD”.

Later Elisha came to Damascus while “Ben-hadad the king of Syria was sick”. The king sent Hazael with forty camels' burden of every good thing of Damascus, to ask through the man of God, “Shall I recover of this disease?” Elisha told Hazael to say that he might recover, but that the LORD had shown him the king would die. Hazael went back and told his master that Elisha had said he would recover.

The next day a thick cloth was dipped in water and spread on his face, “so that he died: and Hazael reigned in his stead”. The verse says only that “he” took the cloth. That is the last Scripture says of him. Whether he is the king who fought Ahab, and how other records tell the change of king, are set out on his page as a ruler.

hazael-1ki-19-15.short: Hazael, sent by his sick master Ben-hadad to Elisha, became king of Syria after him, struck Israel east of the Jordan, and was paid to turn back from Jerusalem.

paragraphs.text: Hazael first appears in the word of the LORD to Elijah at Horeb: “anoint Hazael to be king over Syria”. The same word joined him with Jehu and Elisha: “him that escapeth the sword of Hazael shall Jehu slay”. Scripture does not record that he was anointed, and does not name his father.

When Ben-hadad king of Syria lay sick, he sent Hazael to Elisha with forty camels' burden of gifts, to ask whether he would recover. Elisha “settled his countenance stedfastly, until he was ashamed: and the man of God wept”. He said he knew the evil Hazael would do to Israel: setting their strongholds on fire, slaying their young men, dashing their children and ripping up their women with child. Hazael answered, “is thy servant a dog, that he should do this great thing?”, and Elisha told him the LORD had shown that he would be king over Syria.

Hazael went back and told his master that Elisha had said he would recover. The next day a thick cloth dipped in water was spread on the king's face, “so that he died: and Hazael reigned in his stead”. The verse says only that “he” took the cloth.

As king he was fought by Joram of Israel and Ahaziah of Judah at Ramoth-gilead, where the Syrians wounded Joram. In Jehu's days “the LORD began to cut Israel short”, and Hazael struck all the land east of the Jordan, from Aroer by the river Arnon, even Gilead and Bashan. He took Gath and set his face to go up to Jerusalem; Jehoash king of Judah sent him the hallowed things and the gold of the house of the LORD and of the king's house, and he went away.

Kings says the LORD delivered Israel “into the hand of Hazael king of Syria, and into the hand of Ben-hadad the son of Hazael”, and that “Hazael king of Syria oppressed Israel all the days of Jehoahaz”. Jehoahaz was left only fifty horsemen, ten chariots and ten thousand footmen, for the king of Syria had destroyed them. Then “Hazael king of Syria died; and Ben-hadad his son reigned in his stead.”

Chronicles tells of a Syrian army that came against Joash of Judah and sent its spoil to the king of Damascus, without naming the king. Amos foretold a fire on “the house of Hazael” because Damascus had threshed Gilead. When he reigned, and what records outside the Bible say of him, are set out on his page as a ruler.

ben-hadad-2ki-13-3.short: Ben-hadad son of Hazael followed his father as king of Syria; Jehoash of Israel beat him three times and took back the cities taken from Jehoahaz.

paragraphs.text: Scripture says little of this Ben-hadad, all of it in a few verses. He was the son of Hazael king of Syria, and Kings says the LORD delivered Israel “into the hand of Hazael king of Syria, and into the hand of Ben-hadad the son of Hazael, all their days”. That verse does not call him king.

As Elisha lay sick of the sickness he died of, Joash king of Israel came to him. Elisha had him shoot an arrow eastward, “the arrow of deliverance from Syria”, and then strike the ground; Joash struck three times and stopped, and Elisha said, “now thou shalt smite Syria but thrice”. Elisha's words name no king of Syria.

When Hazael died, “Ben-hadad his son reigned in his stead.” Jehoash son of Jehoahaz took back out of his hand the cities that had been taken from Jehoahaz by war: “Three times did Joash beat him, and recovered the cities of Israel.” Scripture gives him no length of reign and does not tell how his reign ended.

Amos, speaking against Damascus, says: “I will send a fire into the house of Hazael, which shall devour the palaces of Ben-hadad.” Later Kings says that Jeroboam son of Joash king of Israel recovered Damascus for Israel, but it names no king of Damascus. When he reigned, and what records outside the Bible may say of him, are set out on his page as a ruler.

rezin-2ki-15-37.short: Rezin king of Syria joined Pekah of Israel against Ahaz of Judah and besieged Jerusalem, until the king of Assyria took Damascus and slew him.

paragraphs.text: Scripture does not name Rezin's father or tell how he became king. Kings first names him in the closing lines of Jotham's reign: “In those days the LORD began to send against Judah Rezin the king of Syria, and Pekah the son of Remaliah.” He is not the Rezin whose children are named among the Nethinims in Ezra's list of those who came back from captivity.

In the days of Ahaz, Rezin and Pekah came up to Jerusalem and besieged Ahaz, “but could not overcome him”. When the house of David was told, “Syria is confederate with Ephraim”, the heart of Ahaz and of his people was moved “as the trees of the wood are moved with the wind”. Their plan, as the LORD told it to Isaiah, was to set a king of their own in Judah, “the son of Tabeal”.

At that time Rezin “recovered Elath to Syria, and drave the Jews from Elath”. Chronicles, which does not name the king of Syria, says the LORD delivered Ahaz into his hand, and that a great multitude of Judah were carried captive to Damascus.

Isaiah told Ahaz not to fear “the two tails of these smoking firebrands”, and gave the LORD's word on their plan: “It shall not stand.” “For the head of Syria is Damascus, and the head of Damascus is Rezin.” Isaiah also said that the riches of Damascus would be taken away before the king of Assyria.

Ahaz sent the silver and gold of the house of the LORD and of the king's house to Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria, asking to be saved “out of the hand of the king of Syria”. The king of Assyria went up against Damascus, took it, carried its people captive to Kir, “and slew Rezin”. Chronicles adds that the king of Assyria came to Ahaz and “distressed him, but strengthened him not”. When Rezin reigned, and what records outside the Bible say of him, are set out on his page as a ruler.

hiram-2sa-5-11.short: Hiram king of Tyre sent cedar and builders for David's house, and was Solomon's partner in building the temple and in his fleets.

paragraphs.text: Hiram was king of Tyre. He sent messengers to David with cedar trees, carpenters and masons, “and they built David an house”. Kings says “Hiram was ever a lover of David”. Scripture does not name his father or say how long he reigned.

When Solomon was anointed king, Hiram sent his servants to him. Solomon asked for cedars out of Lebanon for the house of the LORD, since none in Israel could hew timber “like unto the Sidonians”. Hiram “rejoiced greatly”, blessed the LORD for giving David “a wise son over this great people”, and promised to bring the timber by sea in floats to the place Solomon named. Chronicles calls him Huram; in his letter he blesses “the LORD God of Israel, that made heaven and earth”, and names the port as Joppa.

Hiram gave Solomon cedar and fir, and Solomon gave him twenty thousand measures of wheat and twenty measures of pure oil year by year. “There was peace between Hiram and Solomon; and they two made a league together.” Solomon's builders and Hiram's builders hewed the stones and prepared the timber together. In Chronicles Solomon promises the hewers twenty thousand measures each of wheat and barley, and twenty thousand baths each of wine and oil.

When the house of the LORD and the king's house were finished, Solomon gave Hiram twenty cities in Galilee. Hiram came out from Tyre to see them, “and they pleased him not”; he asked, “What cities are these which thou hast given me, my brother?”, and called them the land of Cabul. Kings then says he sent the king sixscore talents of gold. Chronicles speaks instead of cities which Huram had restored to Solomon, which Solomon built and settled with Israelites.

Hiram sent seamen who knew the sea with Solomon's servants from Ezion-geber to Ophir, and they brought back gold: four hundred and twenty talents in Kings, four hundred and fifty in Chronicles. His navy brought almug trees and precious stones from Ophir, and Solomon's navy of Tharshish sailed with Hiram's, coming once in three years with gold, silver, ivory, apes and peacocks. He is not the other Hiram, a widow's son of the tribe of Naphtali, whom Solomon fetched out of Tyre to work in brass. When he reigned is set out on his page as a ruler.

queen-of-sheba-1ki-10-1.short: The queen of Sheba heard of Solomon's fame, came to Jerusalem to test him with hard questions, blessed the LORD, and went home.

paragraphs.text: Scripture never gives her name: Kings calls her “the queen of Sheba”, and Jesus speaks of “the queen of the south”, who came “to hear the wisdom of Solomon”. She heard “of the fame of Solomon concerning the name of the LORD”, and came to test him with hard questions. She came to Jerusalem with a very great train, with camels that bore spices, very much gold, and precious stones.

She “communed with him of all that was in her heart”, and Solomon told her all her questions. When she had seen his wisdom, the house he had built, his table, his servants and ministers, and his ascent to the house of the LORD, “there was no more spirit in her”. She told him the report she had heard in her own land was true: “Howbeit I believed not the words, until I came, and mine eyes had seen it: and, behold, the half was not told me.”

She said, “Happy are thy men”, and blessed the LORD his God, “which delighted in thee, to set thee on the throne of Israel”. She gave the king a hundred and twenty talents of gold, precious stones and a great store of spices, and Kings says there came no more such abundance of spices. Solomon gave her all her desire, whatever she asked, and she went back to her own country with her servants.

Chronicles tells the same visit in nearly the same words. Its account of why she came does not speak of the name of the LORD, and in her blessing the LORD sets Solomon “on his throne, to be king for the LORD thy God”.

Jesus said the queen of the south will rise up in the judgment with this generation and condemn it, “for she came from the uttermost parts of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon; and, behold, a greater than Solomon is here.” Luke gives the same saying. Scripture does not say where Sheba lay, who her family were, or what she did after she went home. Where her land may have been, and the names later writers gave her, are set out on her page as a ruler.

mesha-2ki-3-4.short: Mesha king of Moab, a sheepmaster, paid Israel tribute in lambs and rams, rebelled after Ahab died, and was besieged by three kings at Kir-haraseth.

paragraphs.text: Scripture names Mesha once: “Mesha king of Moab was a sheepmaster”, who paid the king of Israel a hundred thousand lambs and a hundred thousand rams, with the wool. When Ahab was dead, Moab rebelled against Israel. The rest of the chapter calls him only “the king of Moab”.

Jehoram king of Israel went out against him with Jehoshaphat king of Judah and the king of Edom, by the way of the wilderness of Edom, and after seven days' journey they had no water. Elisha told them to make the valley full of ditches, and said the LORD would fill it with water and “deliver the Moabites also into your hand”.

Moab gathered all that were able to put on armour and stood in the border. In the morning the sun shone on the water, and the Moabites saw it “as red as blood”; they said the kings had struck one another, went for the spoil, and were routed. The allies beat down the cities, covered every good piece of land with stones, stopped the wells and felled the good trees, until only Kir-haraseth was left, with slingers around it.

When the king of Moab saw that the battle was too sore for him, he took seven hundred swordsmen to break through to the king of Edom, “but they could not”. Then he took his eldest son, who should have reigned after him, “and offered him for a burnt offering upon the wall”. “And there was great indignation against Israel: and they departed from him, and returned to their own land.”

Scripture does not name Mesha's father or his capital, 2 Kings 3 does not name the god to whom he offered his son, and Scripture does not tell what became of him after Israel went home. When he reigned, and what records outside the Bible say of him, are set out on his page as a ruler.

candace-act-8-27.short: Candace was queen of the Ethiopians; Acts names her only to say whose treasurer was the eunuch whom Philip baptized on the road to Gaza.

paragraphs.text: Scripture names Candace once, and she does not appear in the story herself. Acts names her to say whose officer the traveller was: “an eunuch of great authority under Candace queen of the Ethiopians, who had the charge of all her treasure”.

Her treasurer had come to Jerusalem to worship, and was going home in his chariot reading the prophet Isaiah when Philip, sent by the angel of the Lord to the road from Jerusalem to Gaza, joined him. Philip “preached unto him Jesus” and baptized him, and the eunuch “went on his way rejoicing”.

Scripture tells no more of her: not where in Ethiopia she reigned, nor whether she heard of her treasurer's baptism. Whether “Candace” was her own name or a title, and what other ancient writers say of the queens of the Ethiopians, are set out on her page as a ruler.
